Appreciation of evidence and reasons for decision 18.

After going through the evidence and circumstances of the case as well as arguments advanced on behalf of the prosecution and by the Ld counsel for the St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha accused, it emerges that the complainant Sh. Vijay Kumar Singh /PW1 reported the matter to the police vide complaint exhibit Ex. PW1/A on the basis of which FIR Ex. PW10/A was recorded and investigation was launched.

19. To prove the commission of offences punishable U/s 420, the prosecution has produced Sh.
Vijay Kumar Singh / complainant as PW1 who has deposed that accused misrepresented him and dishonestly induced him to sell Patanjali Products to the accused by saying that accused was running a shop in the name of Komal Enterprises which was a GST Registered firm.

He further stated that believing the assurances given by the accused to make payment of the products from time to time, he supplied the Patanjali Products to the accused and for the payment of the same, the accused issued cheques to him which subsequently got returned with remarks "insufficient Funds"
and therefore, the complainant has alleged that the accused had committed cheating with him.
20.

The accused is charged with commission of offence u/s 420 IPC for which the ingredient are:-
1. Deception of any person.

(a) Fraudulently or dishonestly inducing that person - (i) to deliver any property to any persons or (ii) to consent that any person shall retain any property or (b) Intentionally inducing that person to do or omit to do any thing which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property.
St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha 21.
Section 420 IPC is a form of cheating that includes inducement in terms of delivery of any property as well as valuable security.

For an offence of cheating to be made out, it needs to be proved that:-
(i) The representation made by the person must be false.
(ii) The accused had prior knowledge that the representation he made was false.

State vs Anil Kumar Jha on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13449436/
7
(iii) The accused made false representation with dishonest intention in order to deceive the person to whom it was made.

(iv) The act where the accused induced the person to deliver the property or to perform or to abstain from any act which the person would not have done or had otherwise committed.
22. One of the most important ingredients for constituting offence of cheating is deception.
Deception can be done to induce the other person to either deliver or retain the property or to commit an act or omission.
Deceiving means to make a person believe what is false to be true or to make a person believe what is true to be false by using words or by conduct.
23. In deception, a fraudulent representation or willful misrepresentation of a fact is made directly or indirectly with an intent to commit the offence of cheating.

In order to prove the offence, it is not only important to prove that a false representation was made by the accused but also that the accused had a knowledge that the representation was false and willfully made in order to deceive the prosecutor.
If the accused knowingly makes a representation which is false then the accused can be liable for offence of cheating under IPC.
St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha 24.
When one person uses deceitful practices to convince the other person to agree on anything which is harmful to that person, it is known as inducement.
It generally occurs when two parties enter into a contract and the party uses fraudulent inducement to gain advantage on the other party.
The fraudulent inducement can be done when a person persuades another by giving false information about a thing to be beneficial for that person but in reality, it is not.

Fraudulent inducement differs from fraud as inducement needs a person to convince the other person for the object which he wants to achieve and the latter needs the person to commit a deceitful conduct by himself for the object which he wants to achieve.
25.
The most critical aspect of the offence of cheating is that dishonest intention should be present at the time of making the promise.
The presence of dishonest intention is important to hold a person guilty of the offence.
The fact that dishonest intention was present at the time of making the promise is to be proved in order to hold accused guilty for the offence of cheating.
Dishonest intention at the time of making the promise cannot be inferred by subsequent non fulfillment of promise.
The offence of cheating has an element of fraudulent or dishonest intention from the very beginning.
When a party makes a false representation to another party in order to gain some profit, the intention to honour the promise at the time of false representation is presumed to be absent.

26. The discussion on the law relating to the offence of cheating makes it amply clear that in order to bring home the guilt of accused for offence of cheating St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha punishable U/S 420 IPC, the prosecution is duty bound to establish that the accused has by causing deception of the complainant, fraudulently and dishonestly induced him to part with any property to any person or has consented the retention of any property to any person or that by way of intentional inducement State vs Anil Kumar Jha on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13449436/
8

of the complainant, he was made to do or cause omission of an act likely to cause damage or harm to the doer of the act in body, mind, reputation or property, which he would not have done or have omitted to do, had he not been deceived by the accused.
27. Therefore, the intention on behalf of the accused to cheat the person is a pre condition for the offence U/s 420 IPC.
For an offence of cheating it is essential that the deception played by the accused must be from the very inception and the malafide intention should be clearly deductable.

It is also required that the complainant must prima facie establish that due to the act of the cheating,
the complainant has suffered a wrongful loss and the same has resulted in wrongful gain for the accused.
In the absence of these elements, no proceedings U/S 420 IPC are permissible in the eyes of law.

28. As per the deposition of complainant/PW1 on 25.08.2017, a bill in the sum of Rs. 3,15,875/- was raised against the accused for the supply of Patanjali products and the accused issued the cheque dated 02.09.2017.

Again, the accused came to his shop for the supply of further Patanjali products and he supplied the goods having GST and the accused assured that the earlier cheque would be cleared on presentation and the complainant supplied the goods worth Rs 2,58,599/- and against this said invoice, accused issued cheque dated 12.09.2017.
The accused St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha again came to his shop on 04.09.2017, and the complainant supplied the goods worth Rs. 2,79,620/- and the accused issued cheque dated 15.09.2017.
The complainant has deposed that when he presented the said cheques i.e. EX.P1 to P3, on various dates, all the cheques were dishonoured with the remark of 'insufficient funds'.
It has come in evidence that complainant/PW1 raised total bill in the sum of Rs. 8,54,094/- but the accused made a payment of Rs. 50,000/- only on two occasions through NEFT.
After the dishonour of cheques, the complainant tried to contact the accused, but his whereabouts were not known even to the relatives and the mobile number of the accused was switched off.

He approached the police and made a complaint EX.PW1/A and on the basis of which the FIR was registered and the investigation was commenced and the cheques were taken into custody vide memo, EX.PW1/B.
29.

The testimony of Shri Laxman Singh/PW3 and Shri Pankaj Kumar/PW4 leads to inference that they supplied the Patanjali goods from the shop of complainant I.e V.K traders to the shop of Komal Enterprises of the accused.

From the testimony of Gaurav/PW7, it is observed that he was the salesman of the shop of the complainant i.e. V.K traders and he introduced the accused to the complainant and accused took Patanjali products from complainant worth Rs.8,54,000/- and accused issued him cheques and all the cheques got returned dishonoured.
In his cross-examination, he has denied the suggestion that material was given to the accused and he had paid the amount of Rs.8,54,000/- in cash.
St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha 30.

The prosecution witnesses, PW8/HC Anil Kumar, PW9/Ct.Mohan, PW10/SI Omveer and PW 11/Inspt. Ajay Kumar have proved the formal investigation of the case and arrest of the accused and proved the custody of the documents produced by the complainant.

State vs Anil Kumar Jha on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13449436/
9 31.

However, after going through the prosecution evidence on record and arguments advanced by Ld. APP and by the Ld. Defence Counsel, there is no dispute regarding the identity of the accused,
and there is no dispute about the issuance of cheques by the accused as alleged by the complainant.
There is also no dispute that the said cheques were dishonoured for want of sufficient funds when presented by the complainant.

Now the question for determination is as to whether the ingredients of section 415 IPC are fulfilled, so as to attract the provisions of section 420 IPC.
32.
Evidently, the complainant has filed cases U/s 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act against the accused for dishonour of checks.
On perusal of the evidence, there is nothing to show that the accused had intentions at the very beginning to not to pay the invoice amount.

Rather, admittedly,
the complainant/PW1 has deposed that he received Rs.50,000/- twice from the accused through NEFT.
The complainant has already availed his remedy of recovery of amount as mentioned in the cheque by filing cases in the concerned court.
There is no evidence to impute mens rea upon the accused from the very beginning from the time of purchasing of Patanjali products.
No doubt the cheques were dishonoured, but by no means, it can be said that the accused had intentions to cheat the complainant from the very beginning.
St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha 33.
The present case is simplicitor a case of non payment for the products purchased by the accused and the same cannot be a basis for initiating criminal proceedings for offence of cheating.

It has been time and again, reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that when the dispute between the parties was ordinarily a civil dispute resulting from the breach of contract on the part of the accused,
the same would not constitute the offence of cheating in the present case also, the accused has tried to return the money and has taken the defence that he had paid the amount in cash to the complainant.

Though, the defence taken by the accused regarding payment of amount in cash has not been substantiated, however, to inculpate him for the offence of cheating, there is nothing to show that the accused was having mens rea to not to pay for the products purchased by him, from the very beginning.

There is no evidence to show any misrepresentation made by the accused due to which the complainant was duped and there is nothing to show that the accused was not in the business of selling Patanjali Goods.

His Firm Komal Enterprises, has been projected to be selling the goods to it's end customers and the prosecution has not alleged that the said firm was a fake firm only to cheat the complainant or any other person.
It is simplicitor the case of non payment by the accused.
Since, the criminal complaint U/s 138 of NI Act is already filed, the accused would suffer the consequences of offence U/s 138 NI Act if proved against him.

34. The discussion made above is clearly suggestive of the fact that the complainant has miserably failed to establish the essential ingredients for St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha establishing commission of offence U/S 420 IPC by the accused.

Accordingly, accused Anil Kumar Jha is hereby acquitted for offence U/S 420 IPC.
35.

Surety, if any stands discharged.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Section 420 IPC is a form of cheating that includes inducement in terms of delivery of any property as well as valuable security.
For an offence of cheating to be made out, it needs to be proved that:-
(i) The representation made by the person must be false.
Deception can be done to induce the other person to either deliver or retain the property or to commit an act or omission.
Deceiving means to make a person believe what is false to be true or to make a person believe what is true to be false by using words or by conduct.
23. In deception, a fraudulent representation or willful misrepresentation of a fact is made directly or indirectly with an intent to commit the offence of cheating.
In order to prove the offence, it is not only important to prove that a false representation was made by the accused but also that the accused had a knowledge that the representation was false and willfully made in order to deceive the prosecutor.
If the accused knowingly makes a representation which is false then the accused can be liable for offence of cheating under IPC.
When one person uses deceitful practices to convince the other person to agree on anything which is harmful to that person, it is known as inducement.
It generally occurs when two parties enter into a contract and the party uses fraudulent inducement to gain advantage on the other party.
The fraudulent inducement can be done when a person persuades another by giving false information about a thing to be beneficial for that person but in reality, it is not.
The presence of dishonest intention is important to hold a person guilty of the offence.
The fact that dishonest intention was present at the time of making the promise is to be proved in order to hold accused guilty for the offence of cheating.
Dishonest intention at the time of making the promise cannot be inferred by subsequent non fulfillment of promise.
The offence of cheating has an element of fraudulent or dishonest intention from the very beginning.
When a party makes a false representation to another party in order to gain some profit, the intention to honour the promise at the time of false representation is presumed to be absent.
27. Therefore, the intention on behalf of the accused to cheat the person is a pre condition for the offence U/s 420 IPC.
For an offence of cheating it is essential that the deception played by the accused must be from the very inception and the malafide intention should be clearly deductable.
It is also required that the complainant must prima facie establish that due to the act of the cheating,
the complainant has suffered a wrongful loss and the same has resulted in wrongful gain for the accused.
In the absence of these elements, no proceedings U/S 420 IPC are permissible in the eyes of law.
Evidently, the complainant has filed cases U/s 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act against the accused for dishonour of checks.
There is no evidence to impute mens rea upon the accused from the very beginning from the time of purchasing of Patanjali products.
No doubt the cheques were dishonoured, but by no means, it can be said that the accused had intentions to cheat the complainant from the very beginning.
St. Vs. Anil Kumar Jha 33.
The present case is simplicitor a case of non payment for the products purchased by the accused and the same cannot be a basis for initiating criminal proceedings for offence of cheating.
Though, the defence taken by the accused regarding payment of amount in cash has not been substantiated, however, to inculpate him for the offence of cheating, there is nothing to show that the accused was having mens rea to not to pay for the products purchased by him, from the very beginning.
There is no evidence to show any misrepresentation made by the accused due to which the complainant was duped and there is nothing to show that the accused was not in the business of selling Patanjali Goods.
Since, the criminal complaint U/s 138 of NI Act is already filed, the accused would suffer the consequences of offence U/s 138 NI Act if proved against him.
